newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark at highest in 1990s on "new era" economy.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark at highest in 1990s on "new era" economy.

text.p: The dollar continued its merciless climb against the German mark on Friday, soaring to its highest level this decade as U.S. unemployment sank to its lowest level in almost quarter of a century.

The dollar was also unshackled from recent concern about international coordination to slow its rise after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated late Thursday his view that a strong dollar is in the interests of the United States.
Economic data out Friday reaffirmed the growing belief the U.S. has entered a new era of steady growth and low inflation.

"The jobs data are showing us that Greenspan's Nirvana remains intact," said Joe Prendergast, head of global foreign exchange strategy at CSFB. "Growth is still brisk and inflation is elusive. While it may complicate the outlook for nominal interest rates, the real return on dollar assets is rising."

In his latest testimony to Congress, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said the U.S. economy is displaying the characteristics of the 1950s where growth was buoyant but sustainable because of subdued price pressures.
Data out today showed the U.S. created 316,000 new non-farm jobs in July but average earnings were unchanged.
With the unemployment rate in the U.S. falling to just 4.8 percent in July from 5.0 percent in June, President Bill Clinton said the country was enjoying "economic rebirth."
Clinton cited four straight years of budget deficit cuts and the diligence of the Fed as key to the rosy scenario.
At 1533 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.8603/13 marks, up more than two pfennigs from the close in Europe on Thursday. It set its highest level since November 1989 at 1.8620 earlier.
The dollar has risen almost 9.5 percent against the German unit since early June, exaggerated by concerns about high German unemployment and the effects of European monetary union.

"There was a period today where the dollar was basking the best of all worlds, where the (U.S.) jobs data was showing rapid growth but the bonds were held up by modest earnings data," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
The euphoria was disturbed briefly later as another upbeat monthly report from the National Association of Purchasing Management was marred by a jump in its inflation index in July.

The bond retreated sharply and stocks skidded lower, taking the dollar briefly from its highs, traders said. The effect was only fleeting, however, with any threat of interest rate rises merely protecting the attractive dollar returns, said analysts.

The focus will now shift the Bundesbank's reaction to the latest bout of mark weakness, with speculation rife that it may attempt to shore up the mark by allowing its key money market interest rate to tick higher next week.

Even though the central bank's policy-making council is in summer recess, it left the option open to call a variable rate securities repuchase tender next week. This would allow the market to set the repo rate and a drainage of marks from the local money market by the Bundesbank would create the conditions for a rise in the rate from 3.0 percent at present.
